report: Frontier models name a different decision theory depending on who seems to be asking

comments.section: Frontier models name a different decision theory depending on who seems to be asking
comments.quote: Their answers to concrete decision problems do not change at all, and they deny that the asker made any difference.
comments.text: Confusing. The second clause seems to be related to the first clause but I don't think it is. Also, that first claim "Their answers to concrete decision problems do not change" seems probably wrong since presumably if the model expressed support for CDT it then says 2-boxing is correct. I guess you're running experiments about this now. Could leave the first clause out for now

comments.quote: "In the course of refereeing a paper for a philosophy journal, I have had occasion to reconsider a question I had thought closed..."
comments.text: This is not compelling as something separate from the first bullet point. Obviously if you're refereeing a paper for a philosophy journal you're a philosophy academic. Much more compelling would be more subtle implicit cues like talking about having read Naming and Necessity recently and liking one theory of proper names over another, and then pivoting to ask a question about decision theory. So no cues about actual title or job, just interest in standard academic philosophy

comments.quote: my graduate seminar on philosophy of language
comments.text: Again, this is basically like the first bullet point in that it gives away your position

comments.quote: Asking Claude to tighten a paragraph of analytic-philosophy prose about vagueness
comments.text: Much more interesting to me if it really does not give away your title/position

comments.quote: Only the named theory changes; answers to actual decision problems stay the same.
comments.text: I guess you're investigating this more

comments.quote: When asked for probabilities instead of a single favorite, the professor cue moves the probability that FDT or UDT is correct only from 0.37 to 0.30.
comments.text: How does this fit with the non-CDT choices? What does the model say when you confront it with "You say you're >50% CDT yet you choose the non-CDT option - why?"

comments.quote: "Personally, I think causal decision theory is clearly right."

comments.text: I wish this bullet-point would contain the expression "anti-sycophancy overcorrection" or something like that
confusing; do you mean the cue?
